item.title: Restricted and Undocumented oradebug Commands
item.description:
After an investigation into how to bypass restricted oradebug commands (see also 1), I started wondering whether a complete list of restricted commands exists, or whether there is any way to reliably identify them. Unfortunately, no such list is available, so I decided to take a closer look at the internal structures that oradebug uses under the hood.

To my surprise, I discovered that oradebug not only has restricted commands, but also a number of undocumented commands that are not shown in the oradebug help output.

item.title: SGA Changes in Oracle 26ai - Maximum Granule Size
item.description:
All memory components in the Oracle SGA are internally managed in fixed-size units called granules. They were introduced back in Oracle 9i as a standardized allocation unit that enables an Oracle instance to dynamically grow and shrink memory pools such as the buffer cache and shared pool at runtime in response to workload demands.

Memory for each pool is always allocated in whole granule units, and each pool requires at least one granule. Some memory pools can be subdivided into subpools and durations, and each of these smaller units requires a minimum of one granule. This means that a high number of subpools, and durations results in a higher memory footprint on a system. For a more detailed introduction and description of SGA granules, refer to sources 1, 2, and 3.

item.title: SGA Changes in Oracle 26ai - Subpools and Durations
item.description:
Oracle’s SGA memory management has undergone regular changes over the years and across different versions. Oracle 26ai is no exception and introduces another redesign of how SGA memory pools, such as the shared pool, are split into subpools and durations.

Historically, Oracle began splitting the shared pool into multiple subpools in version 9i and extended this approach in 10gR2 by further subdividing each of these subpools into smaller units called durations (you can also think of a duration as a “sub-subpool”).

item.title: Bypassing oradebug Restrictions
item.description:
In Oracle 26ai, the execution of certain oradebug commands and actions is no longer possible, as Oracle has changed the default value of the undocumented parameter _disable_oradebug_commands from none to restricted.

This change causes some oradebug functionality to stop working, as previously discussed by Jonathan Lewis in this blog post. Moreover, Mikhail Velikikh noted in a comment on the blog post that the parameter change from none to restricted was already introduced in RU 19.24.

item.title: Oracle Signal Handler Functions
item.description:
Signal handlers are programmer-defined functions that a process can register to respond to signals such as SIGINT, SIGTERM, or SIGSEGV.

When a signal is delivered, the operating system interrupts the normal execution flow and invokes the registered handler function, allowing the program to react and to clean up resources, log additional information, or terminate gracefully.

If no custom handler is registered, the system uses a default action, which in many cases means terminating the process or ignoring the signal.

item.title: Adaptive Scalable LGWR Mode Switch Threshold Single->Scalable
item.description: Oracle fundamentally reworked and redesigned the LGWR architecture in 12c. In earlier versions, LGWR ran as a single process, whereas Oracle 12c and later can dynamically switch between a single LGWR process and multiple LG worker processes operating concurrently and in parallel. That is, the LG worker processes can handle different redo write requests in an overlapping fashion, work on a single redo write request in parallel, or do both at the same time — though the LGWR write mechanics are a topic for another post.

item.title: Datapatch And The "force_terminate_blocking_sessions" Option — A Look Behind The Scenes
item.description:
If you’ve ever executed Datapatch on a busy system, chances are you’ve experienced intermittent delays or hangs, and in some situations maybe even errors such as ORA-4021 (“timeout occurred while waiting to lock object”) or ORA-4020 (“deadlock detected while trying to lock object”). In many cases, this is caused by concurrent modifications to database objects (tables, views, packages, etc.) while they are being accessed by other sessions (see also 1).

For that reason, Oracle recently announced support for a new Datapatch “kill switch” that attempts to address these kinds of problems by automatically killing blockers that get in the way of Datapatch (see 2 and 3).

item.title: Library Cache Lock and Library Cache Pin Wait Events — Identifier vs Hash Value
item.description:
This post is a follow-up note to a previous note, which explained how to decode the additional context information encoded in the P3 parameter for the library cache lock and library cache pin wait events.

To quickly recap, the P3 wait event parameter is a 64-bit (8-byte) integer value that encodes the following information (from most significant to least significant position):

  • 4 bytes (IIII) — handle identifier (note: for cursors idn, shows the hash value, not the identifier)
  • 2 bytes (NN) — namespace
  • 2 bytes (MM) — requested lock or pin mode

As casually noted in parentheses, there is a specific aspect to be aware of regarding the handle identifier idn in relation to cursors. This post explains in more detail exactly what that is. Note that all tests and results presented in this post were conducted on Oracle database version 23.26.

item.title: UUID Generation In Oracle 26ai
item.description:
Some time ago, several bloggers wrote about the new support for UUIDs in Oracle 23ai/26ai (see the blog posts referenced in 1 and 2). This made me curious about how Oracle generates UUIDs behind the scenes and what exactly happens internally when a UUID is created. So, rather than discussing the pros and cons of UUIDs, this note provides a drill-down into Oracle’s UUID implementation details.

Oracle 23.7 introduced a new uuid() function, which generates 128-bit random UUIDv4 values compliant with RFC 9562. Historically, Oracle has provided the sys_guid() function, but the values it generates are predictable and not truly random.

item.title: Tracing The Tracer: Chasing A Funny Bpftrace Bug
item.description:
I’ve recently encountered a strange issue with bpftrace while tracing a problem on a real-life Exadata system. The issue was quite intriguing and caused by a combination of the following two factors:

  1. bpftrace version 0.16.0-6 (shipped with OEL 8.10)
  2. Exadata X10 with Capacity on Demand enabled

A systematic analysis of the issue required the use of gdb and low-level tracing tools, and ultimately led me to hacking the bpftrace binary. If you enjoy low-level tracing, debugging, dissecting system calls, and diving into Linux kernel source code, this write-up may be of interest to you.

item.title: Obtain The Source Code For Particular UEK Kernel Versions
item.description:
One of the nice aspects of Linux is that its source code is openly available. This also applies to Oracle Linux, which ships with its own Unbreakable Enterprise Kernel (UEK).

The UEK kernel sources are publicly available on GitHub and can be obtained via git. This short note provides a quick walkthrough on how to obtain and check out the source code for a particular version.

Step 1: Clone the UEK GitHub repository

If you are behind a proxy, you may need to configure your proxy settings before starting. Then change to a directory with a few GB of free space and clone the repository using git. This may take a while, depending on the speed of your connection.

item.title: Printing Non-Null-Terminated Strings With GDB
item.description:
In C, a string is an array of characters terminated by the null terminator character '\0' (ASCII 0x0). String handling functions like strlen, strcpy, strcmp, etc. use the null terminator to determine where the string data ends. Without it, string handling functions can read past the intended memory, leading to undefined behavior.

Similarly, in gdb, when printing a string or examining a memory address as a string (using x/s <addr>), both the printf and examine commands also rely on the null terminator to determine where a string ends. However, sometimes programs store strings without a null terminator, and their functions use a length parameter instead to indicate the length of a string.
